title: HTTP2: flush preface / settings frames when channel become active

timeline.body:
Motivation:

We need to manually flush the channl when it becomes active and we wrote the preface / settigns frame as otherwise the remote peer might never see it.

Modifications:

- Flush after writing preface / settings
- Adjust unit test to verify the new behaviour
- Adjust unit tests to complete mocking everything before the connection is actually established

Result:

Fixes https://github.com/netty/netty/issues/12089

I've read the original issue. IIUC, websockets handler needs h2 preface in order to finish its handshake. However, this is not always required for other use-cases. Let's see what spec says (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7540#section-3.5):

> The client sends
   the client connection preface immediately upon receipt of a 101
   (Switching Protocols) response (indicating a successful upgrade) or
   as the first application data octets of a TLS connection.  If
   starting an HTTP/2 connection with prior knowledge of server support
   for the protocol, **the client connection preface is sent upon
   connection establishment**.

> **To avoid unnecessary latency, clients are permitted to send
   additional frames to the server immediately after sending the client
   connection preface, without waiting to receive the server connection
   preface**.  It is important to note, however, that the server
   connection preface SETTINGS frame might include parameters that
   necessarily alter how a client is expected to communicate with the
   server.  Upon receiving the SETTINGS frame, the client is expected to
   honor any parameters established.  In some configurations, it is
   possible for the server to transmit SETTINGS before the client sends
   additional frames, providing an opportunity to avoid this issue.

Spec allows sending the first request with the preface. It's a frequent use-case for http clients that a request triggers a new connection. Since the request is already ready, it's beneficial to flush everything together. Flush is expensive. Extra flush just for the preface will negatively impact latency of the first request. It may be considered as a performance regression by many users.

my 2c: The logic on top of HTTP2 codec can decide if it needs a flush for the preface or not when channel becomes active, but netty should not always enforce it. Alternatively, we can provide an option for `Http2FrameCodecBuilder` to make this decision at configuration time, but not sure if it's worth it. It's standard practice in netty to do something when the channel becomes active. Having an option on `Http2FrameCodecBuilder` that will work only for the client won't be ideal for a class that is shared between client and server.

reply.body:
Currently netty's http2 client handler *does* flush preface for TLS connections - overwhelming majority of use cases, but  does not with prior knowledge. This is inconsistent and may be surprising - why minor case is handled differently than major one?

For non-TLS (prior knowledge) connections, user handlers are required (and be aware) to flush immediately for http2 spec conformance - even if they have no intention to send requests right away.

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7540#section-3.5

> If starting an HTTP/2 connection with **prior knowledge** of server support for the protocol, the client connection **preface is sent upon connection establishment**.

@normanmaurer I was thinking to do PoC on Netty WebSockets on top of H2C as per spec and see what we can come up with.

Goes here: https://github.com/netty/netty/pull/11192#issuecomment-826350511
@trustin Does Armeria has WebSockets with H2C?

> Currently netty's http2 client handler does flush preface for TLS connections 

@mostroverkhov can you point out where this is happening? I've enabled wire+frame logging for ServiceTalk ALPN example with some extra wire logging after `SslHandler` and I don't see a `FLUSH` after preface: https://github.com/idelpivnitskiy/servicetalk/commit/9ff40cc4823bf12e68898268ec251195223fc785

The sequence of events on the client-side:
1. Write `ClientHello`
2. Flush
3. Read TLS handshake response from the server
4. Write `Finished`
5. Initialize h2 pipeline based on ALPN result
6. Write preface and settings
7. Write outbound headers with `endStream=true` (GET request)
8. Flush

The full log can be found here: https://gist.github.com/idelpivnitskiy/f9b08e5bd2503420288177252f5ae4fe

I also tried to remove ALPN and keep a kind of prior-knowledge mode but with TLS, when h2 pipeline is already initialized before the TLS handshake completes. In this case, because we already know we are going to speak h2 after TLS, the preface and settings are flushed all together with the `ClientHello`. This helps us to avoid an extra flush only for preface. The next flush happens after the client writes a `GET` request. The full log: https://gist.github.com/idelpivnitskiy/3fd1b8ba2a2e429cd7b03109c8c50f2e

> For non-TLS (prior knowledge) connections, user handlers are required (and be aware) to flush immediately for http2 spec conformance - even if they have no intention to send requests right away.

The spec has an additional paragraph that permits sending data immediately after the preface. I'm not saying that the preface has to be delayed in time until after the data are ready. I'm saying that when data are already ready, there is no need to flush right after preface bcz we are permitted to flush after data. Adding automatic flush inside netty will limit netty's flexibility to accommodate the described low-latency use-case.

@idelpivnitskiy Re

> can you point out where this is happening 

There was [test](https://github.com/jauntsdn/netty-websocket-http2/commit/97d037ac8209750a724b8e38483c388760cd2620) failing with timeout - due to preface/settings were probably not flushed for prior knowledge case, while tests with TLS/ALPN (e.g. this [one](https://github.com/jauntsdn/netty-websocket-http2/blob/71ffa08b15a860bd9e7824c5a3a5c968c3417118/netty-websocket-http2/src/test/java/com/jauntsdn/netty/handler/codec/http2/websocketx/ProtocolHandshakeTest.java#L46)) passed successfully - which implies preface was written by flush from `SslHandler` (I may debug/provide details later this week).  Failing test was fixed by [commit](https://github.com/jauntsdn/netty-websocket-http2/commit/668bf0ef26a2f0d2cf7d28b913f708c72c2a0aca). 

> Adding automatic flush inside netty will limit netty's flexibility to accommodate the described low-latency use-case

It makes sense; on the other hand, I do not have strong opinion on whether netty's http2 codec should rely on user handler flushes for protocol processing - so leaving It for maintainers consideration.
@idelpivnitskiy @mostroverkhov I still think flushing should be the "default" behaviour here the same way as flush is the default behaviour for SSL to kickstart the handshake.

I would ask for a way to opt out from this behavior then, we don't want this extra flush in ServiceTalk as it will have negative impact on the cost to establish a new h2 connection. It seems unnecessary for other HTTP clients too.
@idelpivnitskiy sure we can do this... Do you also want to opt-out for this in `SslHandler` for example ?
No, everything works as expected today
ok let me add some config and ping you once done

timeline.body:
```suggestion
            if (flushPreface && ctx.pipeline().get(SslHandler.class) == null) {
```
This avoids redundant flush with TLS connections, in other case `Config.flushPreface(false)` is needed for this much more common case. While `ctx.pipeline().get(SslHandler.class)` construct is uncommon for core netty http codecs, It is still used internally (Http2StreamFrameToHttpObjectCodec, WebSocketServerProtocolHandshakeHandler).

Otherwise I would suggest to change `Config.flushPreface` default to false.

reply.body: Actually I think we should just let it flush always... The `SslHandler` will only propagate the flush if there was really something produced.
+1, flush is expensive only when there are pending data. otherwise, it becomes noop
